nameStory: The barn funnel weaver gets its name from two key traits: where you'll find it and what its web looks like. These spiders love to set up shop in barns, sheds, and other outbuildings, spinning their distinctive funnel-shaped webs in corners and crevices. The funnel part refers to their web's design - a flat sheet with a tube-like retreat where the spider waits to ambush prey.
description: The barn funnel weaver is a medium-sized brown spider that's become one of our most common indoor companions. These spiders have long, sturdy legs and a somewhat flattened body that helps them dart quickly across their sheet webs. Adults typically measure about half an inch in body length, with legs that can span up to an inch and a half. Their brown coloration often features subtle patterns that help them blend into wooden structures and dusty corners.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive flat sheet web with a funnel-shaped tube retreat in one corner - the web feels slightly sticky but not as tacky as an orb web

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized spider with a somewhat flattened, oval abdomen and proportionally long, robust legs that feel sturdy when observed

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Brown to grayish-brown coloration with subtle darker chevron or herringbone patterns on the abdomen that may fade with age

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Sits at the mouth of its funnel retreat, quickly darting out when prey hits the web, then retreating back into the tube

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length around half an inch with legs spanning up to 1.5 inches - noticeably larger than common house spiders

habitat: You'll find barn funnel weavers in human-made structures throughout New England - barns, sheds, garages, basements, and porches are prime real estate. They prefer areas with wooden beams, stone foundations, or concrete blocks where they can anchor their webs in corners and crevices. While they occasionally venture outdoors under decks or in woodpiles, they're most successful in the stable, protected environment of buildings.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as temperatures warm, often moving to new locations and rebuilding webs that may have been damaged over winter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with frequent web maintenance and prey capture - this is the best time to observe their hunting behavior and web structure.
seasonality.fall: Mating season brings increased spider activity, and you may notice more individuals as they search for mates and establish overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults can remain active in heated buildings, though their metabolism slows - webs may appear dustier and less maintained during cold months.

funFact: Barn funnel weavers can live for several years, making them practically ancient by spider standards - some individuals may inhabit the same corner of your barn or basement for up to three years, becoming familiar neighborhood residents.
confusionNotes: Often confused with grass spiders, which build similar funnel webs but prefer outdoor locations in gardens and lawns. Remember: if it's indoors in a building, it's likely a barn funnel weaver; if it's outdoors in vegetation, it's probably a grass spider.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the "domestic house spider" in Europe, this species is actually different from what Americans typically call house spiders (Parasteatoda species), which can cause confusion when reading European field guides or websites.
compareHints: Since barn funnel weavers are the only Tegenaria species commonly found in New England, compare them with grass spiders in the same funnel weaver family. Barn funnel weavers are generally more robust with thicker legs and prefer indoor habitats, while grass spiders are more delicate-looking and stick to outdoor grassy areas. Both make funnel webs, but location is your best clue for identification.
